title: Fair Ranking as Fair Division: Impact-Based Individual Fairness in Ranking

problem.claim: Rankings allocate exposure and economic opportunity to ranked items, raising fairness concerns for items.

gap.claim: Existing approaches link item exposure to relevance, but the choice of link function may be difficult to defend and can still yield unfair rankings.

contributions.claim: Develops an axiomatic ranking-fairness approach rooted in fair-division principles that avoids selecting an exposure-to-relevance link function.
Defines fairness through envy-freeness and dominance over uniform ranking, and proposes a ranking objective related to Nash Social Welfare.
Illustrates the trade-off between impact-based individual item fairness and user utility.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report guarantees for envy-freeness, dominance over uniform rankings for every item, and Pareto optimality.
The authors report that conventional exposure-based fairness can produce substantial envy and highly disparate impact across items.
The authors report empirical control of the trade-off between impact-based individual item fairness and user utility.

narrative_sequence.summary: Rankings allocate exposure and economic opportunity, creating fairness concerns for ranked items.
Exposure-relevance link functions are difficult to justify and may still produce unfair rankings.
The paper introduces fair-division axioms and a Nash Social Welfare-related objective for computing fair ranking policies.
The authors report theoretical guarantees, unfavorable contrasts with exposure-based fairness, and an empirical fairness-utility trade-off.

unknowns: Formal definitions of the axioms and objective are not provided.
The empirical datasets, baselines, metrics, and experimental settings are not specified.
The abstract does not quantify the reported guarantees, envy, disparate impact, or utility trade-off.
